newsitem.title: UK: BOE's George warns against EMU stability council.
newsitem.headline: BOE's George warns against EMU stability council.

text.p: Bank of England Governor Eddie George rejected on Monday suggestions that a European stability council should act as a political counterweight to a future European central bank (ECB), describing it as dangerous.

In an interview with the German business magazine Capital, he said the European central bank's role would be to pursue rigorously its responsibility for maintaining price stability, which would make for a strong euro.
"The problem is that that could give rise to tension between some of the member countries," he said.

"Then I think there is a concern that political pressure could be put on the ECB. And that's why I think the suggestion that even before we start we need a political counterweight to the ECB is quite dangerous and partly explains why the core currencies of Europe are weak against the rest of the currencies in the world."
George said it was just as probable that Britain would meet the convergence criteria for joining EMU as that Germany and France would.
But there would be no dramatic impact on Britain if it remained outside as long as it continued to pursue stability oriented policies.
He described suggestions that London could lose its position as a major financial centre if Britain did not join a single currency as "nonsense."

George said he was concerned about the potential for economic tensions between member countries of EMU as they would be affected in different ways by shocks such as oil price rises or dollar fluctuations.
"If the exchange rates are locked before the economies of the participating countries have converged on a sustainable basis, then tensions are unavoidable," he said.
Asked if he though EMU would go ahead in 1999, the central bank chief replied: "I think 1999 is a prudent planning assumption, but I do not think by any means that it is a certainty."
He expressed concern about some member countries viewing membership of a single currency as a matter of prestige, whether the convergence criteria had been achieved or not.
"This could then result in the euro being a weaker rather than a stronger currency," he said.
